answer: The classical transform on n-bit inputs runs Theta(log n) butterfly layers over Theta(n) stored bits. Each layer of t/2 butterflies and twiddle multiplications halves a length-t transform into two length-t/2 transforms, so the arithmetic per layer is small, but on a tape each layer needs at least one scan of all stored bits, and log n scans of n bits cost Theta(n log n). That is why the front page says the logarithmic factor can only be beaten by cheaper address movement or cheaper butterfly arithmetic. The new algorithm attacks both with two tape procedures. The first is a chunk interchange, which moves two address chunks of width u in O(V u^tau) time with tau = 1 - 2^-50. The second is the layer procedure (sifigeg), which applies one bit of each of D selected chunks at once in O(V d^lambda') time with lambda' < 1, instead of one whole-array pass per bit. Both are recursive: a call at parameter mf makes s calls at parameter f on streams of volume V/W, with s < Wm, so each level of splitting multiplies the cost per unit volume by s/W < m, which gives a fixed power below linear in the parameter. The strict inequality s < Wm comes from a rank count on nested subspace labels that I could not verify in detail. The layer's two-point step is rewritten through a kernel C = aI + bX with C^2 = X. Summing all costs gives O(n (log n)^(1-kappa)) with kappa = 2^-182, which is the saving over n log n. I am confident of the mechanism and the scan argument. I am not confident of the exact rank count or of the constants, which the wiki states as choices.

key_idea.statement: A tape procedure's cost per unit volume grows, at each level of splitting its parameter by m, by the factor s/W, which is below m, so the total cost is a fixed power of the parameter below linear rather than linear.
